title: How Wisdom Became the Property of the Human Race
subtitle: An Anansi story

setting.period: Folk-tale time in an Akan village — a story told for hundreds of years

sources.author: W. H. Barker and Cecilia Sinclair
sources.title: West African Folk-Tales

provenance.rights: The text is our own retelling of a traditional Akan Anansi story, written for Omramo; it does not use the wording of the cited edition. The cited edition is in the US public domain (published before 1931); the authors' death years are not verified and other territories are not verified. Legal review pending (PRD Q23).

culturalReview.reason: A living Akan oral tradition (Anansesem); the story, the names and every kente or symbol drawing need an Akan reader.

geography.lesson: Ghana is a country in West Africa. In the south it is warm and rainy, and tall forests grow there.

culture.lesson: The Akan people call their Anansi tales Anansesem, which means spider stories, and they weave a bright cloth called kente. Long ago, people who were taken across the ocean to the Caribbean and the Americas carried these stories with them, and they are still told there.

moral.lesson: No one can keep all the wisdom. Even a child can teach a wise grown-up.
moral.reflectionQuestion: What is something you know that you could teach a grown-up?

moral: Nobody can keep all the wisdom, and even a child can teach a grown-up.

card.label: Character · the keeper of wisdom
card.title: Father Anansi

traits.text: Not as wise as he thinks

card.body: He wants to be the wisest one of all. In many Akan tales Anansi is a spider, and his name means “spider” in Twi.

portrait.alt: Father Anansi, an old man with a white beard and bright woven cloth, holding a round clay pot.

card.label: Character · Father Anansi’s son
card.title: Kweku Tsin
card.body: He watches and wonders before he speaks. One good idea from him changes everything.

portrait.alt: Kweku Tsin, a boy with wide, bright eyes, peeking out between two big leaves.

tapTargets.title: Precious pot
tapTargets.line: A pot that holds something its owner cares about very much.

cultureNote.label: From Ghana
cultureNote.text: For a very long time, people in Akan villages have shaped pots from clay by hand. Pots like these hold water, food and other things worth keeping.

runs.t: Long ago,
Father Anansi
runs.name: anansi

runs.t: held all the wisdom in the world.
He lived in a
village
at the edge of a great green forest. Every day, his neighbours came knocking at his door.
“How do I mend my leaking roof?” asked one. “When should I plant my yams?” asked another.
Father Anansi always knew. He gave out his wisdom a little at a time, and he loved to be the one everybody needed.

unfolded.alt: At dusk, small houses with glowing windows stand at the edge of a forest. Father Anansi, an old man with a white beard and bright woven cloth, sits at his door while neighbours come to ask his advice.

folded.alt: At dusk, Father Anansi sits at his door in a village of small houses with glowing windows.

runs.t: But one day, a neighbour forgot to say thank you. Another only laughed and said, “Oh, I knew that already!”
Father Anansi
runs.name: anansi

runs.t: ’s pride was stung.
“Then they shall have no wisdom at all,”
he grumbled.
“I will take back every last crumb of it.”
All that day he went from house to house, gathering up every wise thing he had ever given away. He poured it all into a big clay pot, pressed on the lid, and sealed it tight.

unfolded.alt: A forest path at twilight, lit by fireflies. Father Anansi walks ahead with a round clay pot hanging at his neck. Behind him his son Kweku Tsin peeks out between big leaves.

folded.alt: Kweku Tsin peeks out between big leaves on a forest path at twilight.

runs.t: But
Father Anansi
runs.name: anansi

runs.t: ’s young son,
Kweku Tsin
runs.name: kweku-tsin

runs.t: , was watching.
Kweku was a quiet boy who noticed things. Why was his father so busy? Why did he keep patting that pot and smiling to himself?
That evening, as the sky turned purple, Father Anansi tiptoed out of the house. His
precious pot
hung from a rope around his neck. Kweku Tsin slipped out after him, soft as a shadow.

unfolded.alt: A forest path at twilight, lit by fireflies. Father Anansi walks ahead with a round clay pot hanging at his neck. Behind him his son Kweku Tsin peeks out between big leaves.

folded.alt: Kweku Tsin peeks out between big leaves on a forest path at twilight.

runs.t: Father Anansi hurried down the
forest
path. He went on and on, until the houses of the village were far behind him.
The trees grew taller and the shadows grew deeper. At last he stopped beneath the tallest tree of all. Its trunk was wider than a doorway, and its top seemed to brush the moon.
“Up there,”
he chuckled,
“nobody will ever reach my wisdom—nobody but me.”
Behind a broad green leaf,
Kweku
runs.name: kweku-tsin

runs.t: held his breath and watched.

unfolded.alt: Father Anansi clings to the trunk of a huge tree, with a clay pot hanging in front of him. A big yellow moon shines behind the leaves, and a small spider hangs on its thread.

folded.alt: Father Anansi clings to a huge tree trunk with a clay pot hanging in front of him, under a big moon.

runs.t: Father Anansi
runs.name: anansi

runs.t: hugged the trunk and began to climb.
But the pot hung in front of his tummy. He could not get his arms around the tree, and he could not see his feet. Up he went a little way—and the pot swung in his way.
Down he slid. He tried again. He puffed, he grunted, he stretched as far as he could—and the pot swung in his way.
Again and again he tried. Again and again, the pot swung in his way.

unfolded.alt: Father Anansi clings to the trunk of a huge tree, with a clay pot hanging in front of him. A big yellow moon shines behind the leaves, and a small spider hangs on its thread.

folded.alt: Father Anansi clings to a huge tree trunk with a clay pot hanging in front of him, under a big moon.

runs.t: Kweku Tsin
runs.name: kweku-tsin

runs.t: watched from below. He bit his lip. He hopped from foot to foot. At last he could keep quiet no longer.
“Father!”
he called.
“Why not hang the pot on your back? Then it would not get in your way, and you could climb easily.”
Father Anansi
runs.name: anansi

runs.t: stopped. He clung to the tree, quite still. Then, very
slowly
, he turned his head and looked down at his son.

unfolded.alt: Father Anansi clings to the trunk of a huge tree, with a clay pot hanging in front of him. A big yellow moon shines behind the leaves, and a small spider hangs on its thread.

folded.alt: Father Anansi clings to a huge tree trunk with a clay pot hanging in front of him, under a big moon.

runs.t: “All the wisdom in the world is meant to be inside this pot,”
he said.
“Yet my own small son knows a thing that I did not!”
His face grew hot. How foolish he felt! In a huff, he tugged the pot from his neck and flung it away.
Down it fell, down through the dark leaves.
Crack!
It landed on a big grey rock and burst into a hundred pieces.

unfolded.alt: A clay pot lies broken on a rock at the foot of a great tree. Golden specks of light drift up out of it and away over the forest, the village and the hills beyond.

folded.alt: A clay pot lies broken on a rock, and golden specks of light drift up into the night sky.

runs.t: Out floated the wisdom, like sparks of gold.
The night wind carried it over the forest and over the village. It drifted across rivers and mountains and seas, to every land in the world.
A little of it settled on everyone—on farmers and fishers, on grandmothers and on babies.
Father Anansi
runs.name: anansi

runs.t: watched it go. Then he gave a small smile, climbed down, took
Kweku
runs.name: kweku-tsin

runs.t: ’s hand, and walked home.
And that is why no one has all the wisdom, and why everyone has some—even you.
